q-42579.name: Question 1
q-42579.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 6 & -3 \\ -12 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-6) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

q-130482.name: Question 2
q-130482.worked_solution:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
det(K)=det[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1 & -7 \\ 4 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot det[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

- For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

- For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(K) & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1 & -7 \\ 4 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}|\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}|\cdot (-3)(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(15-8)\cdot (-3)(8-9) \\  & =7\cdot 3 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130531.name: Question 3
q-130531.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \\ -3 & 5 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}-2 & -4 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}|+3(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-12+20)+3(24-12)-2(20-6) \\  & =8+36-28 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=\frac{1}{16}.
$$

q-130641.name: Question 4
q-130641.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 103 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 144 & 158\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(2\cdot 158-4\cdot 144) \\  & =-(316-576) \\  & =260\end{aligned}
$$

$|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a & b+2\end{aligned}|=8$,
find 
$|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & b\end{aligned}|.$
q-130777.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & b\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & (b+2)-2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a+3 & (b+2)-2\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ a & b+2\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{8}+|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =8+(-6+6) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
